messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maria was thirty-eight when her boyfriend Jason was beaten nearly to death in the parking lot behind the bar where she worked. She had been pouring drinks, laughing with a regular, and never heard a thing. By the time someone screamed and she ran out, Jason was on the asphalt, his face a ruin of blood and swelling, and two men were gone. The police asked her if she had seen anyone, if she had noticed anything odd, and she had to say no. That no lodged in her throat, and it has been there ever since. In the months that followed, the images of Jason’s face stayed brutally clear—she could see the precise way his left eye was swollen shut, the blood matting his hair—while the moments just before were utterly blank. She had no memory of what she was doing at the exact second the attack started, and that blank space felt like a judgment: she should have sensed something, should have gone outside to check on him. The self-blame grew into something solid, and soon she began to believe that people in general could not be trusted—if she could not rely on herself to protect the person she loved, how could she rely on anyone else? Even Jason felt different now; he was still with her, but the quiet between them was heavy with things neither of them said, and Maria had come to feel that she could not lean on him, because he was already broken by what happened.

At work, Maria learned to keep her face smooth and her voice steady no matter what. She was good at it—a bartender had to be—but it cost her. If a customer started a story about a robbery or a fight, she would excuse herself to the back, her heart hammering. She avoided the news completely; the bar had two televisions always tuned to sports or music videos, and she had to look away whenever a headline flashed about an assault. She also refused to see a therapist, even though her sister urged her. Seeking help felt like admitting that she had done something wrong, and she had a deep, unshakable sense that a stranger could not possibly understand what she had caused. The avoidance became a routine: control her emotions, steer clear of reminders, do not let the images surface. But the images came anyway, mostly at night—vivid pictures that played on loop, always ending with Jason’s broken face and always followed by the same blank, accusing gap. She would lie awake next to him and think that if she had been paying attention, if she had been better, the blank would not exist. That thought made her more certain that she was to blame, and more determined to keep everything locked inside.

Over the months, Maria’s world shrank. She started coming home from work and going straight to bed, not because she was tired but because she could not bear the effort of pretending. Her relationship with Jason became a careful dance of avoidance—they stopped talking about the attack, and Maria stopped asking how he was feeling, because she was afraid the answer would confirm that he blamed her too. She had not had a physical checkup in over a year, and when her sister mentioned a therapy group, Maria changed the subject. Each time she avoided a trigger, she told herself it was the only way to stay functional, but something else was happening: the avoidance reinforced her belief that she was not strong enough to face the truth, and that made the distrust of others—and of herself—sink even deeper. She began to see the world as a place where bad things happened without warning, and where she was the one who had failed to prevent them for her own loved one.

What finally drove her to a clinic was a moment at work. A tall man in a hoodie walked in, and the back of his head, the set of his shoulders, was exactly what she had glimpsed in the parking lot that night. She froze, dropped a glass, and when it shattered she started shaking so hard that her manager sent her home. That night, she told Jason she needed help. She is terrified of what will happen if she actually talks about the images and the blank spaces—she fears she will fall apart—but the idea of staying the same is worse. She hopes, vaguely, that someone can tell her how to stop feeling like the whole thing was her fault, though a part of her is sure they will tell her it was.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows memory leading to negative appraisals, but not negative appraisals causing or influencing memory; the required causal direction from Negative Appraisals to Memory is absent.
